newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak parliament approves anti-subversion law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak parliament approves anti-subversion law.

text.p: Slovakia's parliament on Tuesday approved a re-worked draft of a controversial anti-subversion law branded undemocratic by the European Union and United States.
The law, which borrows from communist-era legislation, sets out punishmentS for acts such as organising anti-government demonstrations.

"This law will guarantee that the people dismembering the republic will be put where they belong," said Jan Slota, chairman of the ultra-right Slovak National Party (SNS), a junior coalition partner which initiated the law.
"It is clear (who is meant) when we look at some attitudes of the Hungarian coalition bosses," he added.

Slota said the law was aimed against some activities of ethnic Hungarian leaders, such as their participation in a conference in Budapest last summer which called for cultural autonomy for Hungarian minorities abroad.
Some 600,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Slovakia, mostly on the country's southern border with Hungary, accounting for more than 10 percent of its overall population.
The new legislation has aroused strong opposition within Slovakia, which is seeking early NATO membership, and criticism from Western governments for what is seen as its undemocratic slant.

It was approved by 66 deputies, with five voting against and six abstentions among only 77 deputies present in the 150-seat parliament after a mass walkout by opposition members in protest before the vote was taken.
Those who voted against and abstained were members of the junior coalition partner, the left-wing Workers' Party (ZRS).

The law was originally returned to parliament for review by President Michal Kovac, but the new "compromise" version drops only one clause from the original which would have made it a crime to spread false information abroad.

The new law also replaces the phrase "organising public rallies" with "calling for mass riots" which, its authors say, conforms to European standards. Economically motivated strikes are not recognised as mass riots, the law says.
Slota accused Hungarian ethnic leaders of striving first for ethnic autonomy and, "in the next stage, to cede the southern area of Slovakia".
The law could also be applied to members of other groups in the country, he said, but did not elaborate.

"The new version retains the previous catch-all articles which can be interpreted almost at will and could be easily abused and is aimed against civil rights," Frantisek Miklosko, of the opposition Christian Democratic Movement (KDH) said.
Slovakia has been accused by the EU and the U.S. of foot-dragging on democratic reforms. But Slota said he was not in favour of NATO membership and objected to EU criticisms.
"Joining military components (of NATO) would be a very doubtful move," he said. "What difference will it make whether Russian or American nuclear missiles point at us?"
"I am not essentialy against Slovakia's membership in the EU, but let nobody blackmail us all the time. If somebody thinks Slovaks will kneel at the door begging for (EU) admission, they are wrong."
